claims.claim: Family is a socially recognized group of people, usually joined by blood, marriage, cohabitation, or adoption, that forms an emotional connection and serves as an economic unit of society (OpenStax working definition).

Families can also be built by choice: sociologists note that such families may include groups of close friends or teammates who form strong primary group connections and maintain emotional ties over time.

The family's core functions include care, socialization, emotional support, and economic support; the functionalist view holds that families perform vital roles for society and provide for one another's physical, emotional, and social well-being.

The nuclear family is two parents (traditionally a married husband and wife) and children living in the same household; the extended family is a household that includes at least one parent and child as well as other relatives like grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins.

Single-parent and blended families are common family forms: about 16 percent of U.S. children live in blended families (those with stepparents and/or stepsiblings), and single-parent households have risen as a share of U.S. children's living arrangements.

In the United States, 62 percent of children under 18 live with two married parents (an all-time low), while 26 percent live with a single parent, up from 9 percent in 1960 and 22 percent in 2000 (Pew Research Center, 2023).

Monogamy is the practice of being married to only one person at a time; polygamy is the practice of being married to more than one person at a time and is accepted to varying degrees around the world, almost exclusively as one man married to several women rather than one woman married to several men.

The family life cycle is a set of predictable steps and patterns families experience over time; one of the first designs was developed by Paul Glick in 1955 (growing up, establishing a family, rearing and launching children, empty-nest years).

Families can be sites of strain: as family structure changes, so do the challenges families face — divorce and remarriage create new difficulties, marital problems are often tied to stress (especially financial stress), and abuse can occur between spouses, between parent and child, and between other family members.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'family' should be defined by structure (blood or legal ties) or by function (care and emotional connection).
positions: Some popular definitions center on a particular household configuration, such as two married parents with children.

OpenStax defines family functionally and by social recognition: a socially recognized group that forms an emotional connection and serves as an economic unit, joined by blood, marriage, cohabitation, or adoption — and notes such groups may even be chosen (close friends or teammates).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the attributed OpenStax working definition plus the plain-language version (kinship, marriage, or choice), and states the honest note that family forms vary, without claiming any single form is standard.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate ('Family is a foundational concept in Sociology. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.') asserted no verifiable facts about the family and was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with source-verified content: attributed working definition, four functions, four family forms, marriage patterns, the family life cycle, and the strain note.
Added Pew Research Center (2023) figures on U.S. children's living arrangements; the draft contained no data.
Kept socialization and gender out of scope per the sibling-topic boundaries; each gets a single line or a related-topic link.
